# Augmentation {#sec-augmentation}

Augmentation creates training data from training data: flip an image, crop it, mask part of a
spectrogram, and train on the copies as if they were new. It is usually presented as a bag of
tricks that "add data". Each trick carries an assumption, though: that the transformed copy has
a label you know. That assumption is a claim about the target distribution $p$, and it can be
false. This chapter treats augmentation as what it is on the four levers, a change to the
sampling distribution $q$ that is justified only by an assumption, and measures what happens
when the assumption is true, false, and false but known.

## The problem

Given a transform $T$ of the inputs (a flip, a shift, a mask), training on the pairs
$(T(x), y)$ adds them to $q$. Does that help, and when can it hurt? And what about transforms
that change the label, or mix two examples together?

## Assumptions

1. **A label-preserving augmentation assumes invariance:** $p(y \mid T(x)) = p(y \mid x)$ for
   every transform used, at every strength used. If that fails, the augmented pairs are
   mislabeled examples.
2. **A label-changing augmentation assumes a known effect:** the label of $T(x)$ is a known
   function of the label of $x$.
3. **The demonstration uses a label with exactly known symmetries.** As
   [Data Types and Their Structure](03-data-types.qmd#sec-data-types) noted, real labels rarely
   have invariances that hold exactly. T5's synthetic "side" label does: on the bundled digit
   images, it is 1 when the left half holds more ink than the right. An up–down flip leaves it
   unchanged; a left–right flip reverses it
   ([The Testbeds](../appendix-testbeds.qmd#sec-testbed-t5)).

## Derivation or demonstration

**Augmentation is a change to $q$.** Training on the original pairs plus their transforms
changes the training distribution to a mixture of $q$ and its image under $T$. If assumption 1
holds, every added pair is a pair that $p$ could have produced. The model then sees more of the
target distribution, and its estimate varies less. If assumption 1 fails, the added pairs carry
labels $p$ would not give, which is label noise of a systematic kind
([Labels](02-labels.qmd#sec-labels)).

**Demonstration on T5.** A logistic regression (scikit-learn's defaults, $C = 1$) is trained on
$n$ of the {{< var ch9.n_images >}} digit images with a tie-free side label, and tested on the
rest; 20 seeds. Four training sets:

- **no augmentation;**
- **up–down flips with the same label:** a true invariance;
- **left–right flips with the same label:** a false invariance, since the flip reverses the
  label;
- **left–right flips with the label reversed:** a label-changing augmentation whose effect is
  known.

With $n = 10$ images, test accuracy was {{< var ch9.none_10 >}} without augmentation,
{{< var ch9.inv_10 >}} with the true invariance, {{< var ch9.chg_10 >}} with the label-changing
flip, and {{< var ch9.wrong_10 >}} with the false invariance. With $n = 400$ the four were
{{< var ch9.none_400 >}}, {{< var ch9.inv_400 >}}, {{< var ch9.chg_400 >}} and
{{< var ch9.wrong_400 >}}
(`tests/test_augmentation.py::test_invariant_augmentation_helps_noninvariant_hurts` and
`::test_label_changing_augmentation_helps_when_the_change_is_known`).

::: {.callout-note title="Result: an augmentation is as good as its assumption"}
Augmenting with transforms the target is invariant to adds examples $p$ could have produced. It
never hurt here, and helped most when data was scarce. Augmenting with a transform the target
is not invariant to, keeping the label, adds systematically wrong labels; here it hurt at every
training size, and more data did not close the gap. A transform that changes the label is
valuable once the change is known: labeling the copies accordingly turned the most damaging
augmentation into the most useful one.
:::

{{< include ../includes/cards/invariant-augmentation.md >}}

{{< include ../includes/cards/label-changing-augmentation.md >}}

**Augmentation policies.** In practice, augmentations are applied as randomized policies.
RandAugment reduces a learned policy to two numbers: "N: Number of augmentation transformations
to apply sequentially" and "M: Magnitude for all the transformations", applied to transforms
drawn from a fixed list of 14 [@cubuk2019randaugment, Figure 2]. SpecAugment acts on the log mel
spectrogram of speech with three transforms. Time warping deforms the time axis. Frequency
masking blanks $f$ consecutive mel channels, with $f$ drawn uniformly from 0 to a parameter $F$.
Time masking blanks $t$ consecutive time steps, with $t$ drawn uniformly from 0 to a parameter
$T$ [@park2019specaugment, §2]. Both control the strength of the invariance assumption with a
single magnitude, and the result above says why the strength matters. A transform the target
tolerates when mild can change it when strong: a small shift keeps a digit, while a large one
can push it out of the frame.

**mixup.** mixup trains on mixtures of pairs:
$\tilde x = \lambda x_i + (1 - \lambda)\,x_j$ and $\tilde y = \lambda y_i + (1 - \lambda)\,y_j$, with
$\lambda \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \alpha)$. Its authors frame it as a "vicinal" distribution
around the training data, in the Vicinal Risk Minimization tradition [@zhang2017mixup, §2]. On
the levers it changes both $q$ (new inputs between examples) and the labels (soft ones). Its
assumption is different from a symmetry: the target changes linearly along the segment between
two examples. A test checks the implementation against that definition
(`tests/test_augmentation.py::test_mixup_forms_the_same_convex_combination_of_inputs_and_labels`).

{{< include ../includes/cards/mixup.md >}}

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
Apply augmentation to training batches only, inside each fold, never to validation or test
data. Choose transforms by asking, for each one and each strength, whether the label provably
survives. Where a transform changes the label in a known way, apply the change instead of
dropping the transform.
:::

## What it does to the learned model

A label-preserving augmentation that is true is the cheapest data there is. It moves the model
toward the invariance it encodes and reduces variance, which matters most when $n$ is small. A
false one teaches the model a contradiction: in the demonstration, every image and its mirror
carry the same label although they have opposite true labels. The model can no longer separate
the two cases. Its accuracy then stayed between {{< var ch9.wrong_min >}} and
{{< var ch9.wrong_max >}} across training sizes, against 0.5 for guessing.

## Failure modes

![Panel A: a digit image, its up–down flip and its left–right flip, with the synthetic side label of each (1 if the left half holds more ink). Panel B: test accuracy against training size with no augmentation, up–down flips (a true invariance), left–right flips keeping the label (false) and left–right flips with the label reversed (the flip's true effect); mean and 10–90% band over 20 seeds. An augmentation helps exactly when its assumption about the label is true.](../images/augmentation.png){#fig-augmentation}

@fig-augmentation shows the four training sets side by side. The failures that generalize:

- **A symmetry the task does not have.** A horizontal flip that suits many photographs is wrong
  for text, digits and anything with handedness.
- **A symmetry that holds only at small strength.** Rotating a 6 slightly keeps it a 6;
  rotating it by half a turn makes it a 9. Policies with a single magnitude parameter make this
  a tuning choice, but the choice is still an assumption about $p$.
- **Augmenting the evaluation data.** Test-time inputs are draws from $p$; transforming them
  measures something else.

## What the toy cannot show

The side label is exactly symmetric, so whether an augmentation is right can be decided by
construction. Real symmetries are approximate, partial and strength-dependent, and nothing
measures them except held-out data. The demonstration uses a linear model on tiny images.
Networks that learn their own features may gain more, or less, from the same augmentation.
